input: The inventory policy for a packaging film has been reviewed in order to establish an appropriate level of safety stock, and the analysis draws on the recent demand history for the product in question. Mean demand is 2035 units per week, with a standard deviation of 433 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 5 weeks, so that demand over the lead time averages some 10175 units. On this basis, the safety stock required to support a 95% cycle service level works out at 1598 units, and the corresponding reorder point, at which a replenishment order should be placed, is 11773 units. In practice the stock position is counted against the reorder point at each replenishment review, and an order is placed when the position falls to that point, with the safety stock held back as the buffer against demand running above its average while the order is in transit. It should be noted that the calculation treats demand as being normally distributed and independent from one week to the next, and that seasonal peaks in demand have been excluded from the analysis, so the figures may need to be revisited if the demand pattern changes materially in the future. The policy will then be applied to the film grades covered by the review from the next replenishment cycle onward.
target: Safety stock for the packaging film is 1598 units, set for a 95% cycle service level. The figure rests on the demand record: mean demand of 2035 units per week and a standard deviation of 433 units per week, with a replenishment lead time of 5 weeks. Demand over the lead time averages 10175 units, and the reorder point is 11773 units, the lead-time demand plus the safety stock. The service level is the probability that demand in a replenishment cycle is met from stock; the safety stock is the buffer held against the variability of weekly demand over the lead time, not against its mean. The calculation treats demand as normal and independent between weeks, and seasonal peaks are excluded. The stated stock covers ordinary week-to-week variation at the stated service level; a seasonal peak falls outside the basis of the figure, and cover for a peak would have to be set separately. In operation, the safety stock is not a working balance: it is drawn on only where demand over the lead time runs above its mean, and it is restored by the incoming replenishment. Where weekly demand is correlated rather than independent — a promotion, a contract start, a seasonal build — the variability over the lead time is larger than the stated basis assumes, and the same service level would need a larger buffer. The figure stands as a policy for ordinary variation, to be reviewed when the demand pattern or the lead time changes.
